nameStory: The Silky Rosegill gets its name from two beautiful features that make it unmistakable in the forest. Its cap is covered with fine, silky white hairs that give it a lustrous, almost silvery appearance, while its gills start white but turn a lovely rosy pink as the mushroom releases its spores.
description: The Silky Rosegill is a striking white mushroom that emerges from tree wounds and old knotholes like nature's own silk handkerchief. It starts life wrapped in an egg-like sac that splits open as the mushroom expands, leaving a cup-shaped volva at the stem base. The silky white cap can grow impressively large - up to 8 inches across - and is covered in fine hairs that catch the light beautifully. What makes it truly special are the closely-packed gills underneath that transform from white to pink as the mushroom matures.

idTips.label: Stem Base
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive cup-shaped volva (sac) wrapped around the stem base - this is the remnant of the egg the mushroom hatched from and feels papery to the touch

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: White to pale yellow cap covered in silky hairs that give it a lustrous, almost shimmering appearance when light hits it - feels soft and slightly fuzzy

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Closely spaced gills that start bright white but gradually turn pink as spores mature - they're free from the stem and don't touch it

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Pink spore print that matches the mature gill color - collect spores on white paper to see this diagnostic feature

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always grows from wounds, knotholes, or damaged areas of hardwood trees, especially elms and maples - never on the ground

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: While reportedly edible, never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification - many white mushrooms can be deadly

habitat: In New England, look for Silky Rosegills growing from wounds, old knotholes, and damaged areas of hardwood trees, particularly elms and maples. They prefer older, stressed, or dying trees in both urban and woodland settings. You'll find them growing singly or in small clusters from the tree trunk itself, never on the ground around the base.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin in late spring after warm rains, with small mushrooms emerging from tree wounds as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Silky Rosegills, especially after summer thunderstorms provide the moisture needed for rapid growth from their egg-like stage.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, often producing some of the largest specimens before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period with no visible mushrooms, though the fungus continues growing inside the host tree.

funFact: This mushroom literally hatches like an egg! The entire mushroom starts wrapped in a thin, papery sac underground, then bursts through like a chick breaking out of its shell, leaving the empty 'eggshell' as a cup around the stem base.
confusionNotes: The distinctive volva (cup at stem base) and tree-growing habit separate it from most white mushrooms. However, always be cautious with white mushrooms - some deadly Amanitas also have volvas, but they grow from soil, not trees. Remember: 'Trees are the key' - if it's not growing from wood, it's not a Silky Rosegill.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'rosegill,' this mushroom was recently moved from the Volvariella family classification and is sometimes listed under different family names in field guides. The name 'tree mushroom' is also used for many other wood-growing species, so the silky texture and volva are your best identifying features.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Piggyback Rosegill which grows on other decomposing mushrooms, the Silky Rosegill exclusively grows from living or recently dead hardwood trees. The Silky Rosegill is also much larger and more robust, with more pronounced silky hairs on its cap. Both share the pink gills and volva, but their completely different growing locations make them easy to distinguish.
